facts.statement: The genus Wannia contains only one species, Wannia scurriensis, which is known from a single specimen.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, Wannia scurriensis, which is known from a single specimen.

facts.statement: Wannia was first described by Dr. Wann Langston Jr. in 1949 as a species of Paleorhinus.
facts.quote: Wannia was first described and named by the late Dr. Wann Langston Jr. in 1949 as a species referable to Paleorhinus, P. scurriensis.

facts.statement: The genus name Wannia was proposed by Michelle R. Stocker in 2013.
facts.quote: An alternative generic name, Wannia, was proposed by Michelle R. Stocker in 2013 creating the new combination Wannia scurriensis.

facts.statement: The genus name honors Dr. Wann Langston Jr., and the species name refers to Scurry County where the holotype was discovered.
facts.quote: The generic name honors Langston for his extensive work on archosaur palaeontology, and the specific name refers to the Scurry County where the holotype was found.

facts.statement: Wannia is known only from the holotype TTU P-00539, a partial skull housed at Texas Tech University.
facts.quote: Wannia is known solely from the holotype TTU P-00539, a partial skull preserved in two parts housed at Texas Tech University.

facts.statement: The holotype was collected near Lake Alan Henry in the Camp Springs Formation of the Dockum Group.
facts.quote: The holotype was collected near Lake Alan Henry, 4 km northeast of the town of Camp Springs, from the Camp Springs Formation of the Dockum Group.

facts.statement: The most probable age for the formation containing Wannia fossils is the latest Carnian or early Norian.
facts.quote: Thus the most probable age for the Camp Springs Formation and the lower member of the Santa Rosa Sandstone is latest Carnian or early Norian.

facts.statement: Wannia is classified as the most basal known phytosaur based on five unique traits revealed by its re-description.
facts.quote: However its re-description revealed five autapomorphies, and a phylogenetic position as the most basal known phytosaur, justifying the erection of a new generic name for the species.

facts.statement: Unlike other phytosaurs, Wannia has basitubera at the base of the skull that are widely separated.
facts.quote: Unlike all other phytosaurs, the basitubera, areas at the base of the skull in front of its attachment point with the neck, are widely separated mediolaterally.

facts.statement: Wannia features a swelling on the nasal bone behind the posterior borders of the nares.
facts.quote: A swelling on the nasal bone is present behind the posterior borders of the nares.

facts.statement: Wannia belongs to the parent group Parasuchidae.
Wannia is classified within the family Parasuchidae.
Wannia is classified as a reptile.
Wannia lived during the Norian stage, between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Norian (227.3 to 205.7 million years ago)

rejected.quote: Wannia is an extinct genus of basal phytosaur reptile known from the Late Triassic (late Carnian or early Norian stage) of Texas, southern United States.
